e.t: This noun refers to thorn bushes—plants with sharp, troublesome growth. It occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, in Judges 8:7, and its basic meaning is simply the thorny bushes themselves. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the word’s particular force in that passage cannot be described further. Its use points to a tangible form of plant life rather than an abstract idea or action.

Abiathar is a personal name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The Greek Old Testament uses this name in passages from 1 Samuel through 1 Chronicles. It appears 29 times across 28 verses, with the English rendering “Abiathar.” Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it names the person referred to in each passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s particular role or situation.

Aglath-salisia is a proper name, functioning as the name of a person, place, or other identifiable name-bearing subject. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to identify precisely whom or what it names. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:34. Its exact reference and identity should therefore be understood from that passage’s full context rather than from the name alone.

Adad, also rendered Athath, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies an individual by name. The name appears eight times across eight Old Testament verses, especially in genealogical records in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, and also occurs in 2 Chronicles and Job. Its precise identity in each passage depends on the surrounding genealogy or narrative, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

This verb means to “lift” something or to “remove” it. It can describe taking an object upward, carrying something away, or causing something to be taken out of the way. The central idea is a change in position: something is raised, taken up, or removed. It occurs 260 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its precise sense in a particular verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek noun means “pain,” naming the experience of suffering or hurt. It refers to pain itself rather than describing an action, person, or object. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Psalms and fifteen times in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the experience of pain.

This noun means “seeing again,” referring to the restoration or return of sight. It describes renewed ability to see rather than merely ordinary vision. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 61:1. Because the word appears only there and no verse text is provided, its exact force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. Its central idea remains clear: sight being received again or restored.

This adverb means “without turning round” or “indifferently”—acting without turning back or showing concern. It describes the manner in which someone does something, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is an unresponsive or unconcerned manner, marked by no turning aside. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L701131:identity; p03:word:lxx:L701131:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L701131:reference:0]

This word describes someone or something as “without understanding” or “senseless.” It can function as an adjective describing a person, action, or condition, and as a noun referring to one lacking sound understanding. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs four times, across Psalms, Proverbs, Hosea, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea is the absence of discernment or understanding, rather than merely a lack of information. The surrounding verse determines whether it describes a person or a senseless quality.

This adverb means “from above” or “from upward.” It describes where something comes from or the direction from which it moves, so it commonly points to what is higher than something else. Its exact force is determined by the sentence, but its central idea remains elevation or an upward source. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs 23 times, across Old Testament books and one deuterocanonical book.

This noun means “unbelief”: the absence of trust or confidence in what is believed or declared to be true. It names a settled response rather than an action, describing a condition of not believing. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 14:25. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how unbelief functions in that particular sentence, but the word itself points to the condition of failing to believe.

This Greek LXX noun means “layer,” referring to something laid over or forming one level of a larger whole. It describes a covering or stratum rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition, in Ezekiel 17:6. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a layer or overlying part. This is a rare word in the LXX corpus.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Aroēlis” or “Arilis.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 46:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific family or narrative role cannot be stated safely. Its basic meaning is therefore its use as the proper name of a person in that passage.

This adjective describes something that cannot be swayed, moved, or shaken—something “unswayable” and “unwavering.” It expresses firm stability rather than uncertainty or change. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus and Deuteronomy, where its normal sense concerns being firmly fixed. As an adjective, it describes a person, thing, or condition marked by steadfastness. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described, but the central idea remains dependable firmness.

This word means “immediately” or “on the very day,” emphasizing that something happens without delay, on that same day. It is an adverb, so it describes when an action takes place rather than naming a person, thing, or action. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Proverbs. Its central idea is promptness tied to the day in question: the event is not postponed to a later time.

This Greek LXX noun means “growth,” referring to increase or development. It names the process or result of becoming greater rather than describing a person, place, or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX material represented here, at 2 Maccabees 5:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains growth or increase. This is a noun, so it functions as the name of that developing or enlarging process.

This proper name means “Babylōnian” or “Vavilonian,” identifying something associated with Babylon or its people. It is a name rather than a general action or quality word. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in 3 Maccabees. The exact person, place, or thing identified depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This adjective means “abominable”: it describes something considered deeply detestable or loathsome. It is used as a describing word rather than as the name of a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains something morally or ceremonially repulsive and rejected.

This Greek LXX word is a proper name, rendered “Gadēl; Gathil.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both times in Nehemiah 7, at verses 49 and 58. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, it establishes the name’s identity but does not explain the person’s particular role in either passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Gebōthitēs” or “Yevothitis.” It identifies a person or group associated with that name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:3. Because the word is a name and no English rendering or surrounding verse text is available here, its precise reference must be understood from that passage’s context.

Gelgel is a proper name, referring to a named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is also rendered “Yelyel.” In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, in Ezekiel 10:13. Because the available wording gives only the name and not the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role must be understood from the passage itself rather than from the name alone.

This noun means “muttering”: spoken words or sounds expressing dissatisfaction, usually quietly or under one’s breath. It names the act or expression itself rather than the person who mutters. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, appearing especially in Exodus and Numbers, with additional occurrences in Wisdom, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains dissatisfied or resentful speech.

Daisōn is a proper name, rendered as “Daisōn” or “Theson.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles 1, appearing in the genealogical record. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance; those details would require the surrounding verse text and passage. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it distinguishes one individual within the genealogy.

This Greek LXX verb means “pass the night,” describing the act of remaining through nighttime hours. It is a time-related action rather than a name for a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Job 2:9. Its basic sense is straightforward: someone spends or remains during the night. The surrounding verse determines the precise force of the action, but the word itself centers on passing through the night.

This adjective describes someone or something carrying or equipped with a scythe, a curved cutting tool. Its central meaning is “bearing a scythe.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 13:2. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s specific reference in that passage cannot be described further; its basic lexical sense remains a scythe-bearer or scythe-bearing figure. The word functions as a descriptive term rather than naming an action by itself.

This adjective describes an infiltrator—someone who enters or is placed among others secretly, often with a hidden purpose. It identifies a person by that covert role rather than naming an ordinary, open participant. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, both in Job, at Job 19:12 and Job 31:9. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains a person who has gained access secretly or operates from within.

Ekbatana is a proper name for a place, also known as Ekvatana. It functions as a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:3. The name itself identifies the location; its particular significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Greek LXX verb means “finish off”: to bring something to completion or carry it through to its end. It describes completing an action rather than merely beginning or continuing it. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, once in 2 Chronicles and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains bringing something to its completed end.

Eleēl is a proper name, also given as Elil. It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 8:22 and once in 2 Chronicles 20:14. Because no verse text or surrounding context is included here, the person’s particular role cannot be explained from the name alone. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Eleēl, or Elil, within these two Old Testament occurrences.

This Greek LXX verb means “believe in”—to place confidence in someone or accept that person as trustworthy. It describes an active response of trust rather than merely hearing information or knowing facts. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used across several settings involving people responding with confidence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains personal reliance and trust.

This adjective describes something taken to heart—received inwardly and regarded seriously. It points to an inward response rather than merely hearing or noticing something outwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 75:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: what is taken to heart is accepted as personally significant and held inwardly with seriousness.

This adjective means “taken out,” describing something removed or singled out from among other things. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Genesis 48:22 and Job 5:5. Its basic sense points to something extracted, separated, or specially selected rather than left with the rest. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on removal or on what has been set apart. Its meaning is therefore straightforward but depends on the sentence where it appears.

This verb means “hang upon” or “make dependent upon.” It describes something attached to, resting on, or depending on something else. As a verb, it expresses either the action of causing dependence or the state of being dependent, according to the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 28:7. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains attachment or dependence rather than something standing independently.

This Greek LXX verb means “burn incense” or “offer.” It describes the act of presenting something in worship, especially by burning incense or bringing an offering before God. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing in 1 Kings and Hosea. Its exact object—what is burned or offered—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is a deliberate act of worship or presentation.

This Greek LXX noun means “censure; criticism”—an expression of disapproval or faultfinding directed toward someone or something. It names the criticism itself rather than the person who gives it or receives it. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, across seven Old Testament occurrences and two deuterocanonical occurrences. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being criticized.

Erma is a proper name, rendered as “Erma.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description, so its meaning is chiefly the identity of the named entity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: once in Deuteronomy, twice in Joshua, and once in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence identifies the name but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

This Greek LXX verb means “apt to blush; colour up”—to become visibly red in the face. It describes a physical reaction rather than naming a person, object, or inward idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Esther 5:1. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence around it. Its basic meaning remains the visible coloring or reddening associated with blushing.

This verb means “prosper”: to do well, succeed, or move forward favorably. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it describes favorable progress or success rather than merely existing or continuing. It occurs 58 times in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah, Daniel, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person, plan, or undertaking is being described.

This noun means a “travelling-allowance”: provision or money given to help someone meet the needs of a journey. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 15:14. The word therefore names practical travel provision rather than the journey itself or a person making the journey. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is an allowance supplied for travel.

Zelpha, also rendered Zelfa, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it refers to a named person in the Genesis narrative. The name occurs seven times across seven verses, all within Genesis. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it distinguishes this particular woman from the other people mentioned in the account, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about her role and circumstances.

In the Greek LXX, this noun means “girding”: the act or condition of being girded or fastened around the body. It names a physical form of securing or binding, rather than a person, place, or abstract quality. The word occurs 13 times across the LXX, in Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means to halve something—to divide it into two equal parts. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its precise force in Psalms 54:24 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to show what is being divided and why. The word’s basic idea remains a deliberate division into two equal portions.

Thamasi is a proper name preserved as “Thamasi” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal or place name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Samuel 11, appearing in verses 21 and 22. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its lexical function is clear: it is a named designation, not a general term with a broader ordinary meaning.

This Greek LXX noun means “observation,” referring to the act of looking at or examining something. It describes attentive viewing rather than a command or a personal quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Daniel and three times in 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being observed and the surrounding sentence.

Iethiraios is a personal name, also rendered “Iethireos.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice in one verse, 2 Samuel 23:38. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning or explanation of the person’s identity. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes something as adequate or sufficient—enough for a particular need, purpose, or situation. It can characterize a person, amount, or provision, depending on the sentence around it. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 43 times, showing a broad use for what meets an expected requirement rather than falling short. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being measured or considered sufficient there.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iou” or “Iu.” It identifies a named person or entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 62 times across 57 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Kings. Because it is a name, its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage; the word itself supplies the name, not a broader descriptive meaning.

This noun means a “tracker”: a person who follows or searches by tracing a path or signs left behind. It identifies someone engaged in tracking rather than describing the path, sign, or object being followed. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 14:22. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its ordinary meaning remains a person who tracks or follows a trail.

This verb means “cleanse”: to make something clean. It describes an action performed on a person or thing, rather than naming a condition or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 117 times, showing that cleansing is a recurring biblical action. Its use reaches across passages such as Genesis 35:2 and several laws in Leviticus, while its precise force in any verse depends on what is being cleansed and the surrounding passage.

This verb means to make an attempt on someone or something—to try to attack, challenge, or take action against it. It describes an intentional effort directed toward a target, rather than a vague desire or passing thought. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 13:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the exact force of that attempt must be determined from its immediate context, but the central idea remains a deliberate attempt against a person or object.

This Greek Old Testament word means “flee for refuge”: to escape danger by seeking a safe place or protection. It describes purposeful movement away from threat toward shelter, rather than ordinary travel. In the Septuagint, it occurs 18 times, including passages connected with fleeing to designated places of refuge. The word is a verb, so it expresses the action of seeking safety. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains flight toward protection.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a branding iron, a heated tool used to leave a permanent mark. Its meaning is concrete and specific: it names the implement, not the mark itself or the action of branding. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:22, though the available word-level information does not supply the verse’s surrounding wording.

This word is a proper name, referring to the named Kinaioi or Kinei. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:55. Without the verse text or broader surrounding context, its precise referent cannot be described more fully here; the supported meaning is the name itself: “Kinaioi” or “Kinei.”

This noun means “labor; weariness”—the effort involved in work or the tiredness that work can bring. It can describe demanding exertion, exhausting toil, or the weariness associated with sustained effort. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 34 times, showing a recurring biblical way to speak about the burdens and fatigue connected with labor. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “creation of the world.” It is a noun describing the bringing of the world into existence, or the world’s origin as an act of creation. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:7. Because no verse text is provided, the word’s exact emphasis in that passage cannot be described further, but its central meaning remains the creation or making of the world. It refers to a beginning brought about through creative action, rather than simply to the world as an existing place.

Kyrēnaios, also rendered Kirineos, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named subject in the Greek LXX, but the name itself does not specify further details about that subject. It occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:23. Its precise reference must be understood from that verse and its surrounding text.

This Greek LXX noun means “shining” or “light.” It refers to brightness or radiance, and its basic idea is something that shines or gives light. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Baruch 4:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central sense remains brightness or illumination rather than darkness. This is a rare word in the LXX material, so its normal meaning is best stated simply: shining light.

This Greek Old Testament verb expresses the idea of being or becoming white. It describes whiteness as an action or condition rather than naming a white thing. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Leviticus 13, at Leviticus 13:38 and 13:39. Its basic meaning remains focused on whiteness, while the surrounding sentence determines whether it describes becoming white or being white.

Mareroth is a proper name, rendered “Marerōth” or “Mareroth.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:3. The available wording identifies the name, but without the verse text and surrounding passage, its particular referent and role cannot be explained further here.

Machati, also written Makhati, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Joshua, across three verses. The name is preserved in the passages as a personal or place designation, but the available information does not identify which kind. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself.

This adverb means “magnificently” or “with much magnificence.” It describes an action carried out in a splendid, grand, or highly impressive manner, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the action it modifies, but its central idea is clear: something is done with exceptional grandeur or splendor.

This noun refers to a measure of capacity equal to 10 gallons. It identifies how much a container or quantity holds, rather than describing an object, person, or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Haggai, and Bel and the Dragon. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a standard measurement of volume.

This Greek LXX verb means “commit adultery”: to be unfaithful in the marriage relationship through sexual sin. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where its basic sense concerns marital unfaithfulness. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central meaning remains clear: violating the faithfulness owed within marriage.

Moolam is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 19:33, and is rendered “Moolam.” Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the surrounding verse text, its specific referent must be determined from that passage. The name itself should therefore be understood as a distinct biblical designation, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

“Find flaw/fault” is the basic meaning of this Greek LXX verb. It describes identifying a defect, weakness, or fault in someone or something. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Proverbs and twice in the deuterocanonical books Wisdom and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the act of noticing or pointing out what is defective.

Nephōsasim, also written Nefosasim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. Its meaning is therefore the identification of the person or group bearing this name, not a general concept that can be translated into an ordinary English definition. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 7:52. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify whom the name refers to there.

This Greek LXX noun means “wood” or “timber,” referring to material from trees used as a substance, building material, or object. It can describe wood in its natural state or prepared pieces used for construction and other purposes. The word occurs 291 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing a broad ordinary use rather than a specialized term. Its exact sense in a particular passage depends on how the surrounding verse uses wood or timber.

This Greek LXX verb means to be “aware”—to know, recognize, or understand something. It describes having knowledge of a person, fact, situation, or circumstance rather than merely encountering it. The word appears 172 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is a broad and regularly used expression of knowing. Its exact emphasis may be intellectual awareness or recognition, depending on the sentence in which it appears.

This adjective describes someone who has undergone an experience like another person’s—someone sharing a comparable condition or circumstance. It points to likeness in what people experience, rather than naming a particular emotion, virtue, or event. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is having “of like experience.”

This noun means “navel,” referring to the small central mark or hollow on the abdomen. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for a physical part of the body and occurs four times, in Judges, Job, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. The word itself identifies the body part without adding a broader spiritual or symbolic meaning. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Ossa is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: once in 1 Chronicles 9:16 and again in 1 Chronicles 16:38. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject in each passage.

This noun means “one who fights with snakes.” It identifies a person by the kind of struggle he undertakes, rather than naming a general feeling or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs only once, at Leviticus 11:22. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while the precise force of its use depends on that passage’s context.

This Greek LXX verb means “betray” or “give over”—to hand someone or something into another person’s control, often with the sense of surrendering or delivering it. It can describe betrayal when a person is handed over to an enemy, but the basic idea is transfer into another’s power. The word occurs 218 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing that it is a broadly used action word rather than a term limited to one situation.

This adjective means “paternal”: it describes something connected with a father or with one’s fathers. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs nine times, showing an established descriptive use. Its precise force depends on the noun it describes, but the central idea remains a relationship to the paternal side or to a father’s family line. It describes a quality or connection rather than an action, person, or event.

This verb means “get fat,” describing becoming physically enlarged or well-fed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, and its basic sense remains bodily growth or increased fatness. Because it is an action word, it describes what happens to someone or something rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is becoming fat or growing stout.

This word means “fifty,” the number that comes after forty-nine and before fifty-one. It functions as an indeclinable number, so it identifies a quantity without changing its form. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 146 times, describing counted people, objects, measurements, or groups. Its meaning remains straightforward: whenever it appears, it marks the quantity fifty rather than expressing an abstract quality or action.

e.h: A Word for Broad-brimmed Felt Hat
e.t: This word means “broad-brimmed felt hat”. It is a noun naming a particular kind of hat, distinguished by its wide brim and felt material. The term occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:12. Its basic meaning identifies an item of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there, but the word itself refers plainly to this kind of headwear.

This verb means “multiplied” or “become numerous.” It describes people or things increasing in number, emphasizing growth from fewer to more. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it appears three times, all in Deuteronomy, so its basic sense is consistent rather than broad or varied. The word functions as an action: someone or something becomes more numerous. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains increase in number.

This adjective means “like a saw” or “saw-shaped,” describing something whose form resembles a saw. It is a descriptive word rather than a name for an object, so its role is to identify a visible likeness. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:15. The precise thing being described there belongs to the verse’s surrounding context, but the word itself contributes the clear image of a saw-like shape.

This verb means “look laughing at”—to direct a laughing or amused look toward someone. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it normally tells what someone does with the eyes or expression. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach 13. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a look marked by laughter toward another person.

gl: make to lean against; put against
d: make to lean against; put against

e.t: This Greek verb means to make something lean against another object or to put it against something. It describes an action of positioning or supporting one thing by placing it beside or against another. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:24. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself expresses placing something so that it leans against or rests against something else.

This Greek LXX verb means “inflame” or “incense still more,” describing an increase in burning or in the act of offering incense. Its basic idea is to intensify something already burning or to add further fire. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:11. The exact force in that sentence depends on its surrounding verse, but the word itself points to making a fire or incensing action stronger.

This word means “gate-keeper” or “warder”: a person assigned to guard and attend an entrance. As a noun, it identifies someone responsible for controlling access, watching a gate, or serving at a guarded entry. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 30 times, so it is a recognized occupational or service term rather than a description of a momentary action. Its exact responsibility in any passage depends on the surrounding text, but the central idea remains a person stationed to protect or manage a gate.

Ramah is the name of a place. As a noun, it identifies a geographical location rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 25 times across 24 verses, from Joshua through Zechariah. Because the word is a proper place name, its significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account and from what Scripture says about Ramah there. The name itself simply refers to Ramah.

This word means “measured motion”. As a noun, it can also refer to “time”, especially time understood as an ordered or measured progression. The central idea is movement that follows a recognizable measure or rhythm rather than being random or uncontrolled. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across Exodus, 2 Kings, Wisdom, and Song of Songs. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

Sambri, also rendered Samvri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 29:13. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person. The name should remain distinct as an LXX form rather than being treated as a general Greek vocabulary term.

This verb means to extinguish or quench—to put out a fire, flame, light, or something burning. It can also describe bringing an active force or source of trouble to an end. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 45 times, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages rather than being limited to one setting. The exact object being quenched must be understood from the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains stopping something that is burning, shining, or continuing with force.

This Greek LXX noun means “plank,” referring to a flat, usually substantial piece of wood. It names a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 43:23. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its short definition, while the precise significance of the object in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual wording.

Seōrim, also written Seorim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or family connected with the priestly divisions listed in 1 Chronicles 24:8. It occurs once in this Greek Old Testament corpus, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it names Seorim. The passage reference establishes where the name appears, while the name itself does not provide a broader definition.

This Greek LXX noun means “sowing,” the act of putting seed into the ground for cultivation. It refers to the planting stage of agriculture rather than to the seed itself or the later harvest. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in 2 Kings and once in 1 Maccabees. Its ordinary meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used in a literal agricultural setting or as part of a broader statement about crops and planting.

This Greek LXX noun means “block” or “post,” referring to a solid upright or set piece. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 45 times in the Greek LXX, primarily in Old Testament books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a block or post. It appears from Genesis through 3 Maccabees, showing continued use across the corpus.

This adjective describes people who have been called together or summoned. It points to a gathered group brought together by an intentional call, rather than people who happen to be present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 16:2, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense highlights the act of calling people together and their resulting status as an assembled group.

This verb means “gird”: to fasten or secure clothing or something around the body. It describes an action of preparation, allowing a person to move or work without loose clothing getting in the way. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus 8:7 and once in 1 Maccabees 3:3. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the ordinary meaning remains the act of girding or fastening around oneself.

This noun describes “living with; intercourse”—shared life or close association between people. It can refer broadly to dwelling or being together, while in some uses it points to intimate intercourse. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical writings: once in Wisdom and three times in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and subject being discussed.

This verb means “congregate”—to come together or gather with others. It describes an action rather than a person or thing, pointing to the act of assembling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 22:24. That is its only recorded use in this corpus, while the basic idea remains straightforward: people coming together. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation in which the action appears.

gl: say the same thing with; agree with
d: say the same thing with; agree with

e.t: This verb means to say the same thing with someone else—to agree with that person. It describes shared verbal affirmation rather than merely being silent or inwardly favorable. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 13:1; the single reference identifies its location but does not by itself establish the verse’s full contextual force. Its basic sense is joining another person’s expressed position.

This Greek LXX verb means “make to fall; throw down.” It describes the action of causing a person or thing to fall, or bringing it down by force. The word appears eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used in more than one setting. The surrounding verse determines what is being brought down and how the action functions there.

Sōba, also rendered Sova, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Psalms. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine which individual or location is intended in each passage; that identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Tabeēl, also given as Tavil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Ezra 4:7 and Isaiah 7:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity cannot be explained further; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not the person’s character, role, or significance in those passages.

This adjective means “on the third day,” identifying something by its timing. It describes an event or person associated with the third day rather than naming a separate action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 30:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is a time reference: something occurring or existing on the third day.

This verb means “have a hole.” It describes the condition of something that contains an opening or perforation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, and Haggai. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: something is characterized by having a hole. The surrounding words and verse determine what object has the opening, but the verb itself expresses that condition rather than naming the object or explaining why the hole exists.

This noun means “prejudice” or “assumption”: a judgment or belief formed beforehand rather than from careful understanding. It describes a settled expectation that can affect how someone views a matter or person. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Sirach 3:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is an opinion accepted in advance, before the matter has been properly examined.

This noun means “height” or describes something “on high.” It can refer to physical elevation, such as the height of a structure, or to a high position. The word occurs 116 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used broadly for the idea of height or elevation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but its central meaning remains a measured or perceived highness, whether of an object, place, or position.

Phollathi, also rendered “Follathi,” is a proper name rather than a general word with an abstract meaning. It functions as a name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This form occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:5. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific historical role cannot be explained beyond identifying the proper name itself.

This noun refers to a festoon or a chain used as ornament. It names a decorative hanging or linked adornment rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Chronicles 3—at verses 5 and 16. The precise object intended at either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself points to ornamental chainwork or festooning.

This adjective describes something as “wintry” or “stormy,” expressing the character of unsettled weather. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, at Wisdom 16:29. The word’s central idea is weather marked by winter or storm, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes there.

χορεύω means “dance a round”: it describes the action of moving in a circle or group dance. As a verb, it expresses dancing rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Old Testament books and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on dancing in a rounded or joined movement, while the surrounding verse determines the particular occasion.

This Greek LXX verb means “anoint.” It describes the action of anointing a person or thing rather than naming the person or object involved. The word occurs 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, with 59 occurrences in the Old Testament portion and 3 in deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use shows that “anoint” is its normal lexical sense throughout this corpus.

This Greek LXX adverb means “here,” pointing to a particular place or location. It directs attention to where someone or something is, occurs, or is being considered. The word appears 82 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, so it serves as a normal place-reference word rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central meaning remains a clear reference to a place nearby or under discussion.
